extracted.intended_audience: writers (fiction, nonfiction, genre writers, and those seeking writing community/resources on Reddit)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide to finding and using Reddit subreddits useful to writers for critique, craft advice, publishing information, prompts, research, and motivation. Covers which subreddits to use for particular needs and community‑etiquette to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and follow subreddit rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure to read and follow the rules of the subreddits you visit, or you'll risk your post being deleted—or even having your account banned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before posting, check each subreddit's sidebar/rules and any pinned posts for formatting, post type restrictions, flair requirements, and prohibited content. Noncompliance can lead to deletion or bans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect personal privacy — don't post personal details
rubrics_metrics.description: Reddit is anonymous and very, very public. Don't post personal details unless you want the whole world knowing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sharing identifying information, do not post private contact data, and assume public visibility; this is both a safety and professional/privacy best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect blunt criticism; be emotionally prepared
rubrics_metrics.description: Especially in the writing subs, Redditors don't pull any punches with criticism, and the communities include basically every demographic in the world... so steel your heart and mind before engaging or posting questions, images or written work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate frank feedback, evaluate criticism for usefulness, avoid taking hostile comments personally, and choose critique forums that match your tolerance for bluntness (e.g., destructive vs. constructive communities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with the community — upvote and respond
rubrics_metrics.description: Upvote content you enjoy and engage with other users' posts to encourage activity and community in each sub.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocate by commenting on others' posts, offering feedback where appropriate, and using upvotes to help good content surface; participation increases the likelihood of receiving useful responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right subreddit based on size, personality, and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The differences between subreddits lie in the size, personality, and attitudes you'll encounter in each one—the first is the largest subreddit and community dedicated to writing, but the latter is more typically open to critiques and has more flexible rules around what you're allowed to post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether you want a large general audience, a smaller critique-friendly group, or a niche genre community; read the culture and posting norms before sharing work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use genre-specific subreddits for targeted feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Join genre/form-specific communities (e.g., Fantasy, Mystery, SciFiWriters, WritersOfHorror, YAwriters, Poetry, Screenwriting) to get advice and critique tailored to your genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post in the subreddit most aligned with your work for more informed feedback about genre conventions, audience expectations, and submission outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use critique-focused communities for direct feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities like DestructiveReaders focus on honest, deconstructive critique; WritersGroup aims for constructive peer-review, and some subs are explicitly set up for critique exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a critique sub that matches the tone you want (harsh/honest vs. thoughtful/constructive), and follow that community's guidelines for submitting excerpts, word limits, and critique swaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publication- and agent-focused subs for publishing advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Subreddits such as PubTips, SelfPublish, and Publishing are for discussing publishing—the industry, trends, and practical publishing/self-publishing advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PubTips to post query letters for community critique; SelfPublish for peer experiences about self-publishing process and pitfalls; Publishing for industry-level discussion and trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prompts subreddits for practice, creative exercise, and feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: WritingPrompts (very large) and ScreenwritingPrompts are places to find prompts, flex creative muscles, respond publicly, and receive reactions and feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to prompts is a low-stakes way to practice, experiment with voice, and build an audience; check each prompt's rules (length, content warnings, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research and expert subreddits for factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: AskHistorians, AskScience, and AskScienceFiction offer expert answers for historical, scientific, and speculative questions; these subs often have strict sourcing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these communities to fact-check details and build plausible elements in your fiction; follow sourcing and question-format rules to get reliable answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialized information subs (Worldbuilding, Etymology, ConLangs) as writing tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldbuilding, Etymology, and ConLangs are rich resources for constructed worlds, language history, naming, and fictional language creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tap these communities for deep dives into culture, names, language, and setting details; bring specific, focused questions to get substantive help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine subreddit archives and AMAs for interviews and research
rubrics_metrics.description: AskMeAnything archives contain interviews and Q&As with notable figures and can serve as research sources when you cannot interview someone directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search AMA archives for primary‑source perspectives and quotes relevant to characters, professions, or historical figures you're depicting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use book and literature subs to find comp titles and deeper discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Subreddits like SuggestMeABook, Book Suggestions, Books, and Literature are useful for finding similar titles, comp titles, and participating in deep literary discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe your book as if you're looking for a book and ask for recommendations to get instant comp-title suggestions; join book clubs and discussions to understand reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use idea-mining subs (TodayILearned, NoStupidQuestions) for story starters
rubrics_metrics.description: TodayILearned and NoStupidQuestions are treasure troves for surprising facts, unusual questions, and story ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browse archives for interesting facts or oddities that can seed scenes, character quirks, or plot elements; keep notes of intriguing threads for later use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use motivation and commiseration subs for habit-building and morale
rubrics_metrics.description: KeepWriting, JustWriterThings, and GetMotivated provide motivation, commiseration, and accountability for writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post goals, celebrate wins, and draw on community encouragement during writing sprints or low-motivation periods; these subs are good for routine and morale rather than critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of content‑specific norms (e.g., NoSleep immersion, EroticaAuthors NSFW)
rubrics_metrics.description: NoSleep operates with immersive norms where readers comment as if stories are real; EroticaAuthors is topical and can be NSFW.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect each sub's culture: NoSleep expects in‑character immersion and forbids breaking the conceit; NSFW subreddits require appropriate labeling and may have posting restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use career- and practice-focused subs for professional development
rubrics_metrics.description: FreelanceWriters, Journalism, and TechnicalWriting are communities to discuss career paths, client work, pay, and professional practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek advice on breaking into technical writing, freelancing best practices, industry rates, and journalism norms; these subs often include practical job-related resources and discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand activity level varies—choose active vs. niche accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subreddits (e.g., Nonfiction) are very small and not very active, while others have huge subscriber counts and lots of engagement; WritersGroup is helpful but not terribly active.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want quick responses, prefer larger active subs or those known for critique; for focused, expert replies you may prefer smaller niche subs even if response time is slower.

rubrics_metrics.name: If your genre or form isn't listed, search—there's likely a niche community
rubrics_metrics.description: This is far from a comprehensive list of subreddits for writers, but if you didn't see your genre or form here, try searching for it—you'll likely discover a subreddit full of your tribe waiting to engage with you and help you succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Reddit search, related-subreddit links, and sidebar recommendations to find very specific communities (e.g., niche fandoms, regional writing groups, format-specific forums).
